edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, chapter V, printed p. 45 (PDF page 69)

source_text: Ex quibus ergo Anima corporis expers ostenditur, ex iis potissimum etiam simplex demonstratur. Nam si corpus non est, et omne corpus compositum est; compositum autem ex partibus constet, nec plurium quidem partium erit. Cum autem incorporea sit, simplex erit: quoniam non est composita, neque in partes secabilis.
orientation: The arguments that show the soul is not a body also show that it is simple, since it has no parts and cannot be divided.
pass_a_gloss: From those things, therefore, by which the soul is shown (ostenditur) to be without a share in body (corporis expers), from these most of all (potissimum) it is also demonstrated (demonstratur) to be simple (simplex). For if it is not a body, and every body is composite (compositum), and the composite consists (constet) of parts (partibus), it will not be of many parts (plurium partium) either. But since it is incorporeal (incorporea), it will be simple, since it is not composite nor divisible into parts (in partes secabilis).

choices.why: 'expers' means having no share in; 'bodiless' would be looser.

pass_b_english: The same arguments, then, that show the soul to be without body also show, above all, that it is simple. For if it is not a body, and every body is composite, and what is composite consists of parts, then the soul will not consist of many parts either. And since it is incorporeal, it will be simple, because it is not composite and cannot be cut into parts.
notes: Edition chapter V ('An simplex sit Anima, an composita').
Printed subjunctive 'constet' kept in sense as one more premise of the 'if' chain.
